new_statements.quote: p. 60: '... iambic forms, that is, to forms with an unstressed presyllable and a stressed main syllable. For instance, Thomas (1963: 61) notes that for Jarai and Chru, PMP disyllabic forms with medial *r, *R, *q, or *h usually lose the first vowel, while in most other instances the first syllable vowel is reduced to shwa.' p. 61: '... the initial impetus for these changes was the PC shift to a preference for final stress under MK influence. Once the canonical preference was set for stress on the final syllable, the preconditions had been set up for the restructuring of the Chamic lexicon.' p. 62: '... contact with MK led to a shift of preference from penultimate to ultimate stress, rather than introducing an entirely new stress pattern. ... Roglai, Rade, and Jarai, apparently in contact with languages typologically very much like PC and thus under minimal external pressure to modify the basic word shape, have remained largely unchanged.'

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog rule '01' (final syllable stressed) matches Thurgood's iambic/ultimate-stress Proto-Chamic word shape which he says Jarai has retained; the statement is comparative and implicit for Jarai rather than an explicit synchronic 'stress falls on the final syllable in Jarai' sentence. Text seen only as Google Books snippets: JSTOR open_url blocked (Client Challenge page, 2 attempts), no open full text found elsewhere.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Proto-Chamic shifted from Austronesian penultimate to Mon-Khmer-style ultimate (final-syllable) stress, giving iambic words with an unstressed, reduced presyllable and a stressed main (final) syllable; Jarai (with Rade and Roglai) is named as a language that has kept this Proto-Chamic word shape largely unchanged, i.e. final stress with a reduced presyllable, without the further move to monosyllables seen in Phan Rang Cham or Tsat.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated for Jarai; the discussion is historical/comparative (word-shape drift disyllabic > iambic > monosyllabic), not a synchronic stress rule for Jarai
new_statements.identity_note: Thurgood 1999 treats Jarai as one language, citing the PL (Lafont 1968) and Lee data sources; no dialect is singled out for the stress remarks. Jensen 2013 describes the dialects of his speakers (UT Arlington, Vietnam-origin Jarai) but states the ultimate-stress rule for Jarai generally.
